| [LIT-041](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-041.md) v2 | The Work Capacity of Channels with Memory: Maximum Extractable Work in Percept-Action Loops | Fiderer et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2504.06209](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06209). The paper models agent and environment as coupled finite hidden-Markov channels. It defines the environment's work capacity C_work = max over agent models of ⟨H(A_t\|M_t) − H(S_t\|M_t)⟩_t (in k_BT ln 2 per round) and proves two things. First, for unifilar environments whose percepts ignore actions, the efficient agents are exactly the randomize-and-forget ∩ maximally-predictive ones, and C_work = log\|A\| − h(S). Second, one binary memoryless environment exists where predictive, max-entropy-action and efficient agents form three nonempty, pairwise-disjoint sets: every predictive agent extracts ≤ 0, uniform-random agents extract 1 − h(3/4) ≈ 0.189 bits, and the optimum is ½·log₂(3/4 + 1/√2) ≈ 0.272 bits, reached by a memoryless agent that plays action 0 with probability 1/√2. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-032); worth reading for anyone working on the thermodynamics of prediction or agency. It gives a clean, fully proved extension of the tape-setting results (Boyd–Mandal–Crutchfield 2018) to feedback loops, and a sharp counterexample to "prediction is necessary for efficiency". Read it knowing that the headline "trade-off" is shown by one existence example, that the example's optimum simply forgets everything, and that Table I prints the memoryless-channel capacity with its sign flipped. |
| [LIT-046](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-046.md) v3 | The Computational Foundations of Collective Intelligence | Pilgrim et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2509.07999](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07999). | [LIT-120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-120.md) v2 | Welfare Subjects and Autopoiesis | Bruckner (2025), DOI-10.1017/apa.2025.10006. Bruckner proposes, by abduction and not deduction (§4), that being autopoietic is sufficient, not necessary, for being a welfare subject. An entity is autopoietic when it "sustains, maintains, and renews itself in a way that responds and adapts to its environmental conditions". On this view insentient plants and a hypothetical non-sentient self-maintaining car ("Tessler") are welfare subjects, while engines with governors, thermostats and heat-seeking missiles are not. He answers the charge of absurd obligations in two ways: welfare value may not generate agent-neutral reasons at all, and if it does, the reasons concerning non-conscious subjects are "extremely weak" (Bradford 2023). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-093](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-093.md)); worth reading as the clearest short statement of a welfare criterion that is not based on sentience and admits machines. Read it knowing that its "autopoiesis" is a loose behavioural notion of adaptive self-maintenance, not Maturana and Varela's self-production, and that the line it draws against thermostats is argued as one of degree ("much richer", §6.1) while being stated as one of kind. |
| [LIT-125](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-125.md) v2 | The moral psychology of obligation | Tomasello (2019), DOI-10.1017/S0140525X19001742. Tomasello proposes that the human sense of obligation is "the internalized social/rational pressure from a joint or collective self-regulating agent 'we'… to do what 'we' expect me to" (§3). It arises first, around age 3, inside joint-commitment collaboration with a partner, and then, from about 3–5 years, toward in-group members through collective identification. It is a "self-conscious motivation" whose coercive force is a threat to one's cooperative identity. The support is a synthesis of developmental and comparative experiments, mostly from his own lab, on WEIRD children versus chimpanzees; the paper runs no new experiment. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md)); worth reading as the standard statement of the shared-intentionality account of obligation and, above all, as a treatment. The commentaries by Bratman, Darwall, Gilbert and Pettit, and the response, are where the naturalistic claim is actually contested. The target article alone is a review-cum-hypothesis, not a demonstration. |

| [LIT-146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-146.md) v2 | The Moral Status of Animals | Gruen & Monsó (2003), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/moral-animal/>. The entry reviews five proposed grounds of moral considerability (species membership, human-exceptional capacities, personhood, sentience and agency). Its conclusion is that attempts to establish human uniqueness by capacities are "not the most promising" (§1.2). It then separates *having* moral status from the *weight* of a claim ("showing up on a moral radar screen", §2.2). Weight depends on the value theory adopted for animal interests (hedonism, preference satisfaction, objective list; §2.1) and on the normative framework (rights, which are absolute but generate forward-looking duties when violated, or a multi-factor utilitarianism). It closes with virtue-ethical, feminist, relational and empathy-based approaches that reject argument from capacities altogether (§3). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-181.md)); worth reading as the standard current survey of the grounds and weighing of animals' moral status. It is balanced for most of its length, but §2.2 argues at length for a multi-factor utilitarian view and §3 ends on Gruen's own "entangled empathy", so cite it for the map, not as neutral on the weighing. |
| [LIT-147](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-147.md) v2 | Mental causation via neuroprosthetics? A critical analysis | Pernu (2018), DOI-10.1007/s11229-018-1713-z. The interventionist/difference-making case for nonreductive mental causation from BCIs (List & Menzies 2009; Menzies 2015; Woodward 2008a,b, 2017) misplaces multiple realisation. What the ensemble recordings show is that one cortical-level variable N (the ensemble's average firing) is realised by many single-neuron patterns N1, N2. Each intention M corresponds to one value of N. So the counterfactual contrast "∼M □→ ∼B true, ∼N □→ ∼B false" fails, and neuroprosthetics supports mental causation only by identifying M with N, not nonreductive physicalism. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-091](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-091.md)); Worth reading as a short, precise diagnosis of a specific equivocation in the interventionist BCI argument (multiple realisation at the wrong level). Its scope is limited to difference-making with a proportionality constraint (fn 1), and its identity conclusion rests on a simplified picture of neural decoding that it asserts rather than argues. |
| [LIT-167](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-167.md) v3 | The Organism | Baedke (2025), DOI-10.1017/9781009495035. Baedke treats "organism" as a nexus concept with an organizational dimension and a relational dimension, joined by the various kinds of biological individuality. He argues that the standard "persister" (self-maintenance, closure) criterion cannot single organisms out, because colonies, holobionts and ecosystems meet it too, and that organisms are also "overcomers", able to destabilize and reorganize their own closure. Organisms are then individuated relationally by tracing diachronic causal paths in the unrolled O/E model of Baedke et al. 2021 ([LIT-110](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-110.md)). The overcomer claim rests on three illustrative cases, anglerfish, sea slug and jumping ant, and is asserted, not shown, to hold of organisms only (p. 40). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-148](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-148.md)); worth reading as a compact, open-access and historically well-informed synthesis of the organism/individuality debate, and as the clearest statement of the persister-vs-overcomer distinction. | [LIT-182](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-182.md) v3 | Towards ethical evolution: responsible autonomy of artificial intelligence across generations | Terziyan et al. (2025), DOI-10.1007/s43681-025-00759-9. The paper proposes, without implementation, formalism or experiment, that an AI system which designs further AI systems should pass on one "immutable" principle. The principle is: do not directly harm humanity or violate fundamental human values; monitor and mitigate misuse of your outputs; and make every derivative inherit this principle (p. 12). The mechanisms are a genetic-algorithm analogy, with immutable and mutable "genes", constrained crossover and filtered mutation, together with "temporal cloning". The paper is inconsistent about its central notion. The principle is enforced once by a penalty F = Q − α·P (p. 9) and once by "unbreachable" hard constraints (p. 13). And it is "immutable" only in its architecture, while its ethical content stays "adaptable" (p. 14). | Rejected — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-156](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-156.md)); not worth a reader's time. | [LIT-192](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-192.md) v2 | What's at stake in the debate over naturalizing teleology? An overlooked metatheoretical debate | Nahas & Sachs (2023), DOI-10.1007/s11229-023-04147-w. The paper argues that "naturalizing teleology" serves at least two relatively autonomous projects with different success criteria. One is scientific: whether an organism-centred account improves biology, which requires operationalisable models that may trade truth for usefulness. The other is philosophical: whether organismal teleology reshapes the liberal-versus-scientific naturalism debate about mind in nature, which requires truth but no operationalisation. It applies the distinction to one recurring dispute, the demarcation of teleological systems from dissipative structures. In the scientific context, models "cannot and need not" demarcate (§4.1: Cusimano & Sterner; McShea & Babcock). In the philosophical context, preferences between accounts turn on unstated commitments (§4.2: García-Valdecasas's Aristotelian case for Deacon over the Organizational Approach). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-094](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-094.md)); worth reading as a compact map of organism-centred teleology (the Organizational Approach, Deacon, Walsh, McShea) and for one reusable move, asking which problem an account of goal-directedness is meant to solve.
